title: Erdogan Urges Trump to Keep Iran Talks Alive as Ceasefire Teeters; Ankara's New Marine Parks Draw Greek 'Illegal' Rebuke
subhead: Turkey's president pressed Washington to pursue diplomacy with Iran as the temporary ceasefire stalls, while Ankara's declaration of two Aegean and Mediterranean marine parks triggered a sharp Greek protest — a fresh flashpoint in the two NATO allies' maritime rivalry.

sections.heading: Erdogan-Trump Call: Ankara Pushes Diplomacy as Iran Ceasefire Wobbles
sections.body:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan urged US President Donald Trump in a phone call to pursue talks with Iran to de-escalate tensions and offered Ankara's support for peace efforts, the Turkish presidency said on Tuesday, according to Reuters and Rappler. Erdogan stressed 'the utmost use of diplomacy' and said Turkey hopes the talks continue and will keep backing peace efforts.

The call came as the US-Iran truce frays: a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday that Tehran would shift to a 'fully offensive' military posture because efforts to negotiate a permanent end to the war have stalled, with Washington ruling out extending the temporary ceasefire. Progress toward resuming oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has also stalled. Turkey, which borders Iran and fields NATO's second-largest army, has maintained contact with Washington, Tehran and mediators including Pakistan and Qatar. On Monday, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed the strait's reopening and ceasefire continuation with his Iranian counterpart.

Erdogan and Trump also discussed bilateral ties, the war in Gaza, and the Turkey-Saudi-Pakistan defense pact, per the presidency's statement.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is positioning itself as the indispensable intermediary at the exact moment the US-Iran ceasefire could collapse — a role that raises Ankara's regional stock but also its exposure if the war reignites on its border.

sections.heading: Greece Condemns Turkey's New Marine Parks as 'Illegal'
sections.body:
Greece on Monday condemned Turkey's creation of two vast national marine parks as 'illegal,' accusing Ankara of encroaching on international waters and Greece's continental shelf, according to AFP via Neos Kosmos. Turkey declared the parks through Presidential Decrees dated August 15, published in the official gazette.

The Fethiye-Kas park in the Mediterranean covers roughly 21,700 square kilometres off the southern towns of Fethiye and Kas, while the north Aegean park spans 1,742 square kilometres near the Dardanelles. Athens said the parks extend beyond Turkey's territorial waters and 'has no legal effect,' insisting Greece's own marine parks were created 'in full compliance with the law of the sea' and exclusively within Greek territorial waters.

Left-wing opposition Syriza's secretary-general Rena Dourou said the first park excludes the entire maritime area around the Greek island of Kastellorizo, while the second extends between Samothrace and Lemnos — calling it the latest in a long series of 'Turkish provocations.'
sections.whyItMatters: The marine parks are a new, concrete flashpoint in the Aegean maritime dispute, testing the Erdogan-Mitsotakis rapprochement that began with their December 2023 friendship declaration — and potentially complicating Turkey's broader diplomatic push.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact: Egypt's Entry Still Uncertain Amid Saudi Reservations
sections.body:
Egypt remains the most likely next entrant to the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed August 7 by Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, but its accession is far from certain, India Today reported. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has called Cairo a 'natural partner' and said only 'technical issues' remained before it could join.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said last week that Cairo was 'seriously considering' joining, pending constitutional and legal reviews of the defense obligations. But India Today notes Riyadh has reservations about Cairo, and Egypt is wary of damaging ties with countries including India — a long-standing partner — as well as its own strategic calculations. Egypt controls the Suez Canal and fields Africa's most powerful military, making it a prized addition to the pact some have dubbed an 'Islamic NATO.'
sections.whyItMatters: Whether Egypt joins will determine whether the Mecca Pact becomes a genuine broad Sunni security bloc or remains a three-power core — and it is a live test of Turkey's ability to expand its new defense architecture.

sections.heading: Kurdish Peace Law: Nearly 4,000 Prisoners Could Be Released
sections.body:
Turkey's Kurdish peace law, passed by parliament on August 10, could lead to the release of more than 3,800 prisoners in its first stage, according to Tuncer Bakirhan, co-leader of the pro-Kurdish DEM Party, in an August 15 interview with T24 cited by Bianet. Bakirhan said the law affects 125,000 cases in total, including 75,000 ongoing investigations and prosecutions and 50,000 secret investigations.

Implementation depends on the state confirming the PKK has laid down its arms. Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci told Hurriyet the confirmation process has four stages: the group surrenders its weapons, security agencies verify disarmament on the ground, findings are confirmed by a National Security Council (MGK) decision, and then implementation proceeds. The law excludes intentional killings committed as part of PKK activities and offenses carrying aggravated life sentences committed before June 1, 2005 — meaning PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan and roughly 900 others fall outside its first-stage scope, though Bakirhan said their inclusion would be considered next.
sections.whyItMatters: The peace process is moving from legislation to the hard part — verified disarmament — and the scale of potential releases (nearly 4,000 in stage one) makes it a high-stakes test of whether the PKK will actually lay down arms.

sections.heading: Turkey Expands Libya Footprint as Fidan Meets Haftar
sections.body:
Turkey is expanding its influence in Libya, with Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan meeting eastern commander Khalifa Haftar amid a US-backed push to reunify the country, according to a report carried by MSN. Ankara's access to rival Libyan authorities could strengthen its disputed maritime claims and reshape regional energy planning.

The outreach comes as Libya's capital Tripoli faces spreading civil disobedience over power cuts, with protesters shutting roads, the foreign ministry and telecoms offices against 10-hour daily blackouts, per the global headlines feed. Turkey's dual-track engagement with both the Tripoli government and Haftar's eastern camp positions it as a key external player in any reunification settlement.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey is hedging across Libya's fractured landscape, using its foothold to protect its maritime claims and energy interests — a play that becomes more valuable if Libya reunifies under a single authority.

sections.heading: Erdogan Revives Syria Visit Plans
sections.body:
President Erdogan plans to visit Syria soon, reviving a trip initially scheduled for April but postponed after the outbreak of the Iran war in February, according to a report carried by MSN. Erdogan reaffirmed Turkey's support for stability in Syria.

The visit would follow his August 16 Al Jazeera interview in which he vowed a Syria trip, and comes as Damascus under Ahmed al-Sharaa pursues a security arrangement with Israel while Turkey maintains its own security interests in northern Syria. The timing — with the US-Iran ceasefire uncertain and Israel conducting incursions into southwestern Syria — makes the visit a delicate balancing act for Ankara.
sections.whyItMatters: A high-profile Erdogan visit to Damascus would signal Turkey's intent to lock in its influence in post-war Syria at a moment when the security landscape is shifting rapidly.

bottomLine: Turkey spent the day straddling two fronts: pressing Washington to keep the US-Iran ceasefire alive while Tehran threatens a 'fully offensive' posture, and opening a fresh maritime dispute with Greece over new Aegean and Mediterranean marine parks. The Erdogan-Trump call underscores Ankara's bid to be the region's indispensable mediator, but the marine parks row shows Turkey is simultaneously asserting hard sovereignty claims that strain its NATO ally relationships. Meanwhile the Mecca Pact's expansion hinges on Egypt, the Kurdish peace process moves toward the hard test of verified disarmament, and Turkey deepens its Libya footprint — a day of active diplomacy and new friction, with the Iran ceasefire the single biggest variable.
sources: Reuters, Rappler, AFP via Neos Kosmos, India Today, Bianet/T24, MSN, Hurriyet
